articles.title: After 6 months of war, US must prepare for a future after Iran’s government falls
articles.summary: The IRGC, Mojtaba Khamenei and Masoud Pezeshkian compete for power as Iran's Islamic Republic fights for survival amid escalating war and sanctions.
articles.body: Six months into the war, the central question about Iran’s regime is no longer its missile arsenal, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) ability to menace the Strait of Hormuz, or how long the confrontation can endure. The deeper question is political and historical: Who governs Iran? Is it Mojtaba Khamenei, whose position at the apex of the system remains opaque; Masoud Pezeshkian, whose office of president was never designed to hold sovereign power; or the IRGC, which after decades of accumulating military, intelligence and economic authority may have become the state’s true center of gravity? Iran increasingly resembles not a Shiite theocracy protected by soldiers, but a militarized dictatorship in which the notorious clerical establishment provides ideological cover for the men with guns. The Shiite Republic or Islamic Caliphate of mullahs emerged from the bleak winter of 1979 promising salvation and delivering coercion. Khomeinism turned political Islam into state power and terrorism, proxy warfare and revolutionary expansion into instruments of foreign policy. For nearly half a century, Tehran built armed transnational terrorist networks abroad while suffocating political life at home. IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY Now, this outlaw regime that once dreamed of exporting its revolution is consumed by a more primitive instinct: survival. War serves that purpose. Under its shadow, dissent becomes treason, criticism becomes collaboration and repression becomes patriotism. Washington must reject the regime’s oldest deception: Iran is not the Islamic Republic, and the Islamic Republic has never been Iran. That distinction matters as economic pressure intensifies. Operation Economic Outcast seeks to sever the financial lifelines sustaining the regime and the IRGC, but Iran’s economic deterioration predates this war and cannot be blamed on sanctions alone. Corruption, ideological adventurism, institutional decay and the diversion of national wealth toward repression and regional militancy have exacted their price. COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES Economic pressure may accelerate the regime’s exhaustion, but the deeper crisis is political and psychological: the widening gulf between a society seeking a place in the modern world and a ruling establishment imprisoned by the fears and obsessions of 1979. Another uprising therefore cannot be excluded. No one can predict when humiliation overcomes fear and private anger becomes public defiance; history rarely announces revolutions in advance. Iran is under immense pressure: grievances have accumulated, the regime’s legitimacy has eroded, and successive uprisings have not been erased because repression has quieted the streets. The regime has contained anger, but not the conditions that produced it. Silence should never be mistaken for consent. IRAN PREFERS CONFLICT WITH US OVER PEACE TO SUPPRESS INTERNAL UPRISING, HUMAN RIGHTS ACTIVIST WARNS Yet the collapse of dictatorship and the birth of democracy are different historical events. Between them lies the dangerous terrain of transition. Iran’s next political order must be chosen by Iranians at the ballot box, not manufactured in Washington, Jerusalem, Moscow or Beijing. Nor does every opposition faction carry equal political weight or vision. In my assessment, Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi occupies a distinctive position through his national visibility and advocacy of secular government, territorial integrity and democratic transition. His role and Iran’s constitutional future — republic or constitutional monarchy — must be decided by Iranians. Regime change should restore a nation’s right to choose, not merely destroy an old order. Nor would the Islamic Republic’s collapse automatically bury the ideologies that have poisoned Iranian politics for decades. Islamism, authoritarian Marxism, sectarianism and separatism would compete for the vacuum. Democracy requires citizenship above ideology, national belonging above faction and the state above revolutionary militias. Iran’s transition will be difficult because the Islamic Republic has spent decades destroying the institutions a peaceful transition would need. Washington’s record deserves scrutiny. Successive administrations have oscillated between confrontation and the hope that another negotiation might alter the regime’s character. Diplomacy can prevent wars, but the illusion begins when a tactical bargain is mistaken for strategic transformation. Tehran has learned to negotiate in one room while applying pressure in another, speaking diplomacy while preserving asymmetric warfare. A regime’s method of survival should not be confused with a change in its nature. IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING Tehran may calculate that America’s political calendar will restrain Washington before the November midterms. But Nov. 3 cannot define American national security. Iran is neither a Republican nor a Democratic question: its covert networks, terrorist capabilities and asymmetric retaliation concern the country itself. A regime fighting for survival may become more dangerous as its options narrow. Negotiation may alter Tehran’s tactics, but asymmetric pressure and deniable violence have been tools of its statecraft for decades. Iran’s next political order must be chosen by Iranians at the ballot box, not manufactured in Washington, Jerusalem, Moscow or Beijing. The deeper lesson reaches back to 1979. Washington misunderstood not only the revolutionaries seizing power but the institutional rupture they were about to impose on one of the Middle East’s oldest nations. It was more than an intelligence failure; it was a failure of political imagination. TRUMP IS WINNING EVERY BATTLE IN IRAN—AND RISKING THE WAR THAT MATTERS Nearly half a century later, America should not again imagine only two futures — accommodation with the Islamic Republic or chaos after it. Serious statecraft should prepare for a third: political transition that preserves Iran’s territorial integrity, national identity and continuity as a unified state. The growing security cooperation among the United States, Israel and Arab states belongs within that horizon. Saudi Arabia faces Iran-backed armed groups, including the Houthis, while Israel and Arab governments confront overlapping security threats. Deeper cooperation — and potentially broader normalization through the Abraham Accords — could build a regional order less vulnerable to proxy warfare and transnational militias. US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS Any regional strategy begins with understanding Iran itself. American and Israeli policymakers — and the intelligence communities that inform them — should distinguish democratic Iranian nationalism from Islamist, Marxist, sectarian and separatist movements offering different futures for the country. Iran’s territorial integrity and credible democratic actors should be understood before transition begins, not after institutions collapse. History is unforgiving toward governments that prepare for yesterday’s crisis; the worst morning to search for reliable Iranian interlocutors is the morning after a dictatorship loses control. China embodies the final contradiction. Foreign Minister Wang Yi calls for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and preventing the war from spreading into Yemen and the Red Sea. Beijing’s anxiety is understandable: Middle Eastern energy arteries are also arteries of the Chinese economy. Yet China cannot demand stability while maintaining close ties with Tehran and avoiding confrontation over conduct that undermines it. Beijing wants open shipping lanes without confronting the forces threatening them — a policy that manages symptoms while leaving the disease untouched. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Hormuz, the Houthis, Tehran’s terrorist proxy networks, sanctions and war are not separate crises. They are consequences of the revolutionary order born in 1979, when ideology became an instrument of domestic rule and foreign policy. For decades, the West has confronted those consequences without resolving the underlying strategic problem. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The question after six months of war, therefore, is not merely how it ends, but what begins afterward. Iran’s future belongs to Iranians, but serious statecraft requires contemplating a future beyond the Islamic Republic. For nearly half a century, the world has built its Iran policy around the regime’s presumed survival. Beneath it stands a far older nation seeking to reclaim its political future. America need not write that future. It should ensure that when history next knocks on Iran’s door, Washington is not once again the last to understand what has arrived. articles.title: Cousins found 700 rare baseball cards hidden under a dollhouse in an Ohio attic; the collection later sold for about $3 million
articles.summary: US News: The discovery of century-old baseball cards in an Ohio attic became one of the most remarkable finds in sports collecting. In 2012, cousins clearing o.
articles.body: The discovery of century-old baseball cards in an Ohio attic became one of the most remarkable finds in sports collecting. In 2012, cousins clearing out a family home in Defiance discovered a box containing roughly 700 cards that had remained hidden for decades. The cards were not ordinary keepsakes. They belonged to the rare E98 series from around 1910 and included some of baseball’s most famous names. Their unusually good condition soon attracted experts, turning a forgotten family possession into a collection valued in the millions.How 700 rare baseball cards ended up under a dollhouseThe story began in an attic in Defiance, Ohio, when Karl Kissner and one of his cousins were helping clear out the home of Kissner’s late grandfather. According to the official website of Major League Baseball(MLB), the family property had passed through several generations before it eventually went to their aunt, Jean Hench. After her death, her belongings were left to 20 nieces and nephews.While sorting through the attic in late February 2012, the cousins came across a cardboard box hidden beneath a dollhouse. Inside were roughly 700 baseball cards dating from around 1910. As reported by BaseballHistory, the cards were part of the E98 Set of 30, a small series that featured 30 players and included 17 Hall of Famers in four colour variations.The cards had apparently belonged to Carl Hench, who had run Hench’s Meat Market & Sausage Works in Defiance. As reported by BaseballHistory, he likely kept surplus cards from the business in the attic, where they remained untouched for about a century.This century-old forgotten box contained famous baseball namesThe significance of the discovery became clearer once the cards were examined. MLB reported that the collection included cards featuring Ty Cobb, Honus Wagner, Cy Young, Christy Mathewson and Connie Mack. These were not simply old cards bearing unfamiliar players. Many belonged to some of the most recognisable figures from baseball’s early years.The E98 series itself was unique. MLB noted that it contained only 30 players, with half of them being Hall of Famers. The manufacturer of the series was also unclear, adding another interesting detail to an already unusual collection.The cards had survived in an attic rather than in a carefully managed collection. Instead of showing the heavy wear that might normally be expected from paper items more than 100 years old, many of the cards appeared remarkably well preserved.What made the century-old baseball cards so valuableKissner did not immediately rush to sell the cards. MLB reported that he left them alone for two weeks after finding them while he researched what the family might have discovered. He eventually sent 8 cards to Peter Calderon at Heritage Auctions in Dallas for an expert assessment.Calderon was struck by both the rarity and condition of the cards. The family then sent the entire collection to the Professional Sports Authenticator(PSA), world's largest and most trusted third-party company that authenticates and grades trading cards, sports memorabilia, and autographs, for further examination and grading.According to MLB, PSA had previously authenticated fewer than 700 E98 cards in total, while the cards from this collection were described as the best examples the company had seen. Sixteen Ty Cobb cards from the group received a grade of nine on the 1-to-10 scale. Even more remarkable, a Honus Wagner card received a perfect 10, the first E98 card to receive that grade from the company.The BaseballHistory report identifies the find as the Black Swamp Find, named after the north-western Ohio region where Defiance is located. It reports that the collection ultimately brought an estimated $3 million through Heritage Auctions.The cards worth far more than an ordinary attic collectionThe possible value quickly moved to a value that would have been difficult for the family to imagine when the box was first discovered. MLB initially reported that the complete collection could bring between $2 million and $3 million. The 37 strongest cards alone were expected to fetch about $500,000 at an August auction held during the National Sports Collectors Convention in Baltimore.The collection was not put on the market all at once. Heritage Auctions planned to sell the cards over several years through auctions and private sales. The approach was intended to avoid putting hundreds of valuable cards on the market at the same time.The family also had to divide the discovery among a large number of relatives. According to MLB, the Hench family planned to split the cards and proceeds evenly among the 20 cousins named in their aunt’s will, with most of them agreeing to sell their share.What made the Ohio discovery different from typical attic findsThe story became memorable not simply because the cards were old, but because several unique factors came together. According to BaseballHistory, most attic collections do not contain anything remotely comparable. Many consist of mass-produced cards from the 1980s and 1990s, old programmes or family memorabilia with little resale value.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump's $14 billion 'bargaining chip': Taiwan arms sale looms over Xi summit
articles.summary: US News: A proposed $14 billion US arms sale to Taiwan is emerging as one of the most sensitive issues hanging over US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Ch.
articles.body: A proposed $14 billion US arms sale to Taiwan is emerging as one of the most sensitive issues hanging over US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, with Beijing pressing Washington to keep the deal on hold while Taipei tries to make the case that its security is in US interests.According to a report by the New York Times, Xi is expected to push Trump to continue delaying the package, which includes missiles, anti-drone weapons and air-defence systems. Trump has already held off approving the sale and previously described the deal as a potential “negotiating chip” with China.China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and has consistently opposed US arms sales to the self-governed island. The issue has become particularly sensitive ahead of the Trump-Xi summit in Washington, where the two leaders are expected to discuss trade, technology and other points of friction.Why Taiwan arms are so sensitiveTaiwan relies heavily on US military support as it seeks to strengthen its defences against potential military pressure from Beijing. Xi warned Trump during their previous meeting that mishandling Taiwan could have serious consequences for US-China relations.Xin Qiang, director of the Center for Taiwan Studies at Fudan University, told NYT that Taiwan was the issue most capable of causing relations between Washington and Beijing to deteriorate sharply. He said securing a continued delay in US arms sales could therefore be one of Beijing’s most important objectives.Trump, meanwhile, has treated the weapons package as leverage in negotiations with China. After his May meeting with Xi in Beijing, Trump called the proposed sale a “very good negotiating chip” for the United States.Beijing could also have other ways of signalling its displeasure if Washington approves the sale. Xi could potentially threaten tighter restrictions on Chinese rare-earth exports or indicate that he might skip the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, which Trump is due to host.Taiwan worries about Trump's stanceFor Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, the continued delay is creating a political problem. Lai has pushed for higher defence spending and greater purchases of US weapons, partly in response to pressure from the Trump administration for allies and partners to contribute more to their own defence.Ryan Hass, a former China director at the US National Security Council and now a Brookings Institution fellow, told NYT that Beijing's strategy could be to prolong the process so that China can improve its military position faster than Taiwan can acquire new capabilities.At the same time, the broader US-Taiwan security relationship remains active. Taiwan's defence minister Wellington Koo recently indicated that American military advisers had become more visible during the island's annual Han Kuang exercises.Chen Ming-chi, a deputy Taiwanese foreign minister handling relations with the US, told The New York Times that American officials understood the importance of continued arms sales to Taiwan.Trump has changed his approach to ChinaThe current uncertainty marks a shift from Trump's first term, when his administration approved about $18 billion in arms sales to Taiwan.In his second term, Trump has placed greater emphasis on maintaining pragmatic ties with Beijing. His administration has also reduced public references to Taiwan, with officials including defence secretary Pete Hegseth avoiding the island in some major speeches, NYT analysed.The arms issue is therefore arriving at a particularly delicate moment. Trump and Xi are scheduled to meet in Washington this week, with Taiwan expected to be one of several issues competing for attention alongside trade, rare earths, artificial intelligence and the war in Iran.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann’s big push to make state drug-free
articles.summary: India News: Punjab Chief minister Bhagwant Singh Mann’s government has expanded its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ anti-drug campaign beyond a conventional police crackdow.
articles.body: Punjab Chief minister Bhagwant Singh Mann’s government has expanded its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ anti-drug campaign beyond a conventional police crackdown, combining action against drug networks with prevention in schools, youth engagement, community vigilance and treatment for people battling addiction.The government said the campaign seeks to make it harder to sell drugs, easier for citizens to report peddling, prevent young people from falling into addiction and ensure those affected can access timely treatment. The strategy brings police, teachers, students, community volunteers and health workers into a coordinated anti-drug effort.Between March 2025 and September 2026, Punjab’s Anti-Narcotics Task Force registered 61,824 FIRs and arrested 81,433 people. Authorities seized 3,918 kg heroin, 991 kg opium, 47 tonnes poppy husk, 1,416 kg ganja and 65 lakh tablets and capsules during the period. Punjab Police also conducted 79,293 public meetings to strengthen community participation in the campaign.The government has simultaneously taken the prevention campaign into schools. A 14-week anti-drug curriculum is being taught to 7.5 lakh students across 3,600 schools through trained teachers. In the first phase, nearly 25,000 teachers from 13 districts are being sensitised, with 7,000 already trained in Amritsar, Tarn Taran and Fazilka. The programme aims to help teachers identify early signs of mental-health distress, vulnerability to substance abuse and possible intervention.Youth programmes are also being used to address peer influence and social acceptance of drugs. Schools have been given year-long activity calendars, while colleges are promoting cultural festivals, mental-health clubs, sports and other activities to encourage healthier lifestyles and reduce the stigma around recovery.At the grassroots level, around 1.25 lakh people have joined nearly 15,000 Village and Ward Defence Committees. More than 50,000 members have been trained to use the Nasha Mukti App to report drug-related information and connect people seeking help with government services.Since its launch on March 1, 2025, the safe Punjab whatsApp helpline has received more than 51,000 citizen tip-offs, which the government said helped police make over 25,000 drug-related arrests.The government has also expanded treatment infrastructure, with Punjab currently having 547 OOAT centres, 219 de-addiction centres and 91 rehabilitation centres. Government facilities have been revamped, health workers trained and skilling and creative activities introduced at treatment centres.Admissions to government de-addiction and rehabilitation centres rose from over 12,200 in 2024 to nearly 34,000 in 2025, an increase of more than 170%, according to the government. articles.title: Can the US win the AI cold war with China?
articles.summary: US attempts to slow down Chinese progress on AI through economic restrictions could backfire.
articles.body:
The success of China’s cheap AI technology has clearly worried American AI companies. Industry leaders have openly called on the US government to take action on competition from the Chinese AI industry.

Washington has already imposed various restrictions on the sale of chips to China. Last year, it launched the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at securing supply chains for AI technology that exclude Beijing; 23 states have since joined, along with the European Union. There is now pressure from the US AI industry to ban or restrict Chinese AI models.

It increasingly appears that the two great powers are on the verge of an AI cold war, each building its own camp and bidding to set the rules of the AI era. The question now is: Having declared this war, can the US win it?

At present, the US and its allies hold the upper hand in several key areas of AI development. China’s frontier AI models remain heavily dependent on imports, chief among them chips, chip-designing software, and chipmaking equipment.

As a result, US export controls hinder China’s ability to keep pace with the latest AI technologies; they drive up costs and undermine investor confidence. They will, however, not hold China’s AI development back forever.

It is important to remember AI development is by no means a single contest over chips; human capital, financial capital, market size, regulatory agility, and industry adoption matter just as much. In response to US export controls, China is not only investing in domestic alternatives but also improving AI model architecture, optimising AI training and inference efficiency, and squeezing more out of the chips it already has.

While trying to catch up with development in chips, China is seeking various loopholes in US export controls to circumvent the restrictions. In June, the US government curbed the ability of Chinese companies to buy advanced US chips via overseas subsidiaries. This loophole was closed, but new ones will emerge.

Whether the US can contain China’s advancement in AI also hinges on the willingness of its allies to cooperate. Advanced chips are not made in a single country. Instead, their supply chain spans multiple political entities, bringing together US design, Dutch and Japanese equipment, and Taiwanese manufacturing.

This dependence means that US export controls, if pushed too far, revised too often, or kept in place for too long, could backfire. US allies, unhappy that Washington keeps offloading steep commercial costs onto them for the sake of its own national security, may well develop policy fatigue and begin actively investing in alternative supply chains to bypass US technology and regulations altogether.

Christophe Fouquet, CEO of the Dutch chipmaking equipment giant ASML, has questioned restricting sales of the most advanced chipmaking equipment to China – under US pressure – would even work or would only push it to redouble its efforts to develop its own.

Doubts about the current US strategy have been voiced even within the US AI industry. US chip giant Nvidia, for example, is against the chip export restrictions, as China is a major market for the company. CEO Jensen Huang has called export controls a “failure” that has cost US companies billions.

Moreover, Chinese open-source AI models have become indispensable to the US tech industry. This year, nearly 200 US startups sent letters to the Trump administration arguing that banning access to advanced Chinese AI models – which tend to be open-source – rather than regulating it would cripple US startups and leave the US market in the hands of a few AI giants. As with all monopolies, the result would be stifled innovation, a diminished US lead in AI, and higher prices for US consumers.

In the AI cold war, China is not just playing catch-up. It is also wielding significant leverage over the US.

Rare earths, which are key to chipmaking, are probably Beijing’s strongest card. The country not only holds the world’s largest reserves of rare earths but dominates their mining and processing. It alone accounts for 91 percent of global rare earths separation and refining production.

Washington is well aware of this. Last year, in response to the renewed trade war, Beijing flexed its rare earths muscle by banning the export of heavy rare earths to the US, which dealt a heavy blow to US manufacturing. It forced Washington to call a quick truce – one that saw Beijing suspend the ban for a year.

Since then, the US has redoubled its efforts to wean itself off Chinese rare earths – to no avail. Not only are Chinese clay deposits – from which rare earth-bearing ores are extracted – more economical than those found in the US or its allies, but China has also mastered the ability to process those ores into rare earths, a capability long spurned by the West because of the pollution it generates.

Although the technology is hardly rocket science, the US and its allies lack the human capital and technology to catch up quickly. China has tens of thousands of experienced engineers working on rare earths processing; in the West, there are just a handful of such experts.

In light of this, should the US escalate its measures against China, it would itself be hit with embargoes and tariffs – measures that would also hinder its own AI development.

Worse still for Washington, rare earths are also used in weapons ranging from F-35 fighter jets to anti-ballistic missile defence systems. Given that fighting between the US and Iran could flare up again at any moment – and that the US army has nearly drained its interceptor stockpiles in the previous round – Washington cannot afford to enter the next round unprepared.

As much as the US would like to restrict China’s AI advance, doing so could be too costly for its own industry. Despite efforts to decouple, “Chimerica” – a term coined to describe the economic symbiosis between the two – is here to stay. The sooner Washington realises that the US needs China as much as China needs the US, the better – not just for both countries, but for the whole world, which could otherwise be caught in the crossfire when these two superpowers duel.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: World leaders descend on New York for UNGA — but who really has America’s ear?
articles.summary: Over 100 world leaders descend on the United Nations General Assembly as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine dominate the diplomatic agenda.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS, NEW YORK — More than 100 presidents and prime ministers will descend on New York this week for one of the busiest gatherings on the diplomatic calendar, arriving at a United Nations confronting wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, economic pressure from disrupted energy markets and fresh questions about the institution’s ability to respond to an increasingly fractured world. The U.N. expects 73 heads of state and 45 heads of government, alongside 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told reporters Friday. Member states have already submitted roughly 1,000 requests for bilateral meetings, while 168 events are scheduled during high-level week, according to Dujarric. Asked Friday to characterize the atmosphere inside U.N. headquarters as the delegations prepare to arrive, Dujarric described it simply as "high stress." INDIA'S MODI-IRAN MEETING COMES AMID US WARNINGS OF SANCTIONS ON TEHRAN'S TRADING PARTNERS The General Debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly begins Tuesday, Sept. 22, under the theme, "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all." But beneath the speeches, motorcades and closed-door meetings across Manhattan is another competition: nearly every government represented in New York will be trying, in one way or another, to capture the attention of the United States. "This is their moment to grab a piece of American mindshare for sure," Frank Ahrens, head of BGR Analytics, told Fox News Digital. A new analysis released ahead of UNGA attempts to measure which countries already have it. The 2026 BGR Impact Index, produced by BGR Analytics, the data practice of Washington-based BGR Group, ranks 197 countries and economies according to their overall footprint in the United States, combining economic, cultural, diplomatic, institutional and geopolitical measures. Japan holds the top position for a third consecutive year, followed by Germany, Canada, the United Kingdom and South Korea. That competition is especially consequential this year. TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS President Donald Trump will return to the General Assembly on Tuesday with the US-Iran war entering its seventh month, while fighting involving the Iran-backed Houthis has placed new pressure on shipping through the Red Sea and raised fresh concerns among Gulf states about regional security. Reuters reported Sept. 18 that European and Asian allies have largely resisted U.S. calls to become more directly involved in the Iran conflict and that the prolonged war has strained Washington’s relationships with some partners. The stakes extend well beyond Iran. The General Assembly agenda is expected to be dominated also by Russia’s war against Ukraine, Israeli-Palestinian tensions, Sudan, climate change and artificial intelligence. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov are among the prominent leaders or representatives expected to speak. That combination of military power, diplomatic access and public perception gets at the central question behind BGR’s index: what does influence actually mean? BGR compiled more than 100 indicators, ranging from GDP, population and foreign investment to international students, cultural presence and lobbying activity in Washington. But one of the most consequential variables in this year’s analysis came from a much newer arena: social media. "We looked at 4.9 trillion pieces of data across an entire year because we know that a social media campaign can really move a country's perception in the U.S.," Ahrens said. "And that was really the big takeaway from this year's index." Social-media sentiment accounts for 20% of the index, second only to cultural imprint at 24%. Institutional ties and outward orientation each make up 16%, geopolitical nexus accounts for 10%, economic size 8% and lobbying and Washington influence 6%. BGR says its underlying data comes from publicly available sources, primarily the U.N., U.S. government agencies and established research institutions, while its social-media data is supplied by Meltwater. For smaller countries, the analysis suggests reputation can produce particularly large swings. Bahrain was the biggest riser, climbing 22 places, from No. 97 in 2024 to No. 75 in 2026. BGR attributed much of that increase to improved U.S.-facing online sentiment and increased visibility tied to Bahrain’s election to a rotating U.N. Security Council seat, its Arabian Gulf Cup victory and a USS Nimitz port call. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS MORE THAN $1B IN UN BUDGET CUTS AS REFORM PUSH GAINS MOMENTUM Georgia moved in the opposite direction, falling 31 positions, from No. 73 to No. 104. BGR said its deteriorating U.S.-facing online sentiment coincided with political unrest and arrests of journalists and opposition leaders. Ahrens acknowledged that generating attention is not the same as wielding political influence. "Countries that make a lot of noise about themselves do get on the radar, but to stay on the radar, you have to have real accomplishments." The index attempts to address that distinction by combining sentiment with harder measures such as economic links, institutional rankings, lobbying expenditure and participation in international organizations. Perhaps BGR’s most unusual example of how national perception can change did not come from a president, diplomat or lobbying operation. It came from a German soccer fan. BGR calls it the "Freddy Effect," after a German World Cup visitor whose enthusiastic posts about traveling through the United States went viral this summer. Ahrens said BGR found that positive sentiment toward Germany increased 13% over roughly three weeks during Freddy’s rise online. BGR links a substantial part of that increase to the reaction generated by his posts, although the data does not independently establish that he alone caused the change. "Can you recreate a Freddy? I don't know if you can reverse engineer him to that effect," Ahrens said. "But what it shows you is how authentic communication really breaks through on social media." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It is a lesson that may resonate with delegations arriving in New York this week, where hundreds of leaders will have only a few days to secure meetings, shape headlines and make their country’s case.

articles.title: Attorney busts ‘biggest misconception’ in Karmelo Anthony filing that could be key in track meet murder case
articles.summary: Karmelo Anthony's 75-page filing of alleged threats, gun photos and violent texts may never have reached jurors, a Texas defense attorney says.
articles.body: A 75-page court filing detailing alleged threats, gun photos and violent text messages tied to convicted Texas killer Karmelo Anthony appears at first glance to be a roadmap of evidence prosecutors planned to present at trial. But a veteran Texas criminal defense attorney says one of the biggest misconceptions surrounding the document is that jurors were never guaranteed to see any of it. Fox News Digital recently obtained the filing, which prosecutors submitted before Anthony's murder trial under Texas Rule of Evidence 404(b). UNTAPPED KARMELO ANTHONY EVIDENCE CACHE SHOWED HE STALKED EX-GIRLFRIEND, HAD 'KNIVES' OBSESSION: PROSECUTORS The filing has taken on renewed importance because Anthony's bid for a new trial focuses on an alleged pretrial agreement governing character evidence. Anthony argues confusion over that agreement affected his decision not to testify, while prosecutors dispute that claim. The notice catalogs dozens of alleged prior acts prosecutors said they may seek to introduce, including allegations that Anthony stalked his girlfriend hours before fatally stabbing 17-year-old Austin Metcalf at a Frisco high school track meet on April 2, 2025. Prosecutors also cited text messages in which Anthony allegedly said he was "on the verge," posed with firearms, made violent threats and repeatedly discussed fighting. KARMELO ANTHONY PHOTOGRAPHED WITH GUNS AS DOCS REVEAL ALLEGED HISTORY OF RAGE, THREATS AND VIOLENCE The filing also includes allegations that Anthony talked about committing robberies, buying firearms and extended magazines, selling narcotics and threatening multiple people, including his then-girlfriend, in text messages spanning several years. Prosecutors also cited screenshots they said represent only portions of larger conversations and noted the alleged prior acts were separate from the charged offense. To some readers, the filing might appear to be a blueprint of the prosecution's case. KARMELO ANTHONY DEFENSE RESTS, ATTORNEYS PREP FOR CLOSING ARGUMENTS BEFORE JURY DELIBERATES IN MURDER TRIAL But appearances can be misleading. Tiffany Burks, a partner at Texas law firm Varghese Summersett and a former prosecutor, said that's not how Rule 404(b) works. TEXAS JUDGE WHO PRESIDED OVER KARMELO ANTHONY MURDER TRIAL REMOVED FROM CASE OVER 'GOT IT RIGHT' COMMENT Burks explained that filing a Rule 404(b) notice does not mean jurors will ultimately hear the evidence. Instead, it gives the defense advance notice of evidence prosecutors may seek to introduce, so attorneys have time to investigate the allegations and prepare a response before trial. KARMELO ANTHONY BLASTS JUDGE IN NEW FILING OVER HANDLING OF MURDER TRIAL If prosecutors believe they may want to introduce evidence of prior alleged bad acts, they must notify the defense before trial, so attorneys have an opportunity to investigate the allegations, prepare a response and avoid being surprised before a jury. "The law requires that you file a 404(b) notice so that you can give the other side notice of what it is you may want to put in trial because the parties have to be prepared," Burks said. "Specifically, the defense has to be prepared to respond or rebut that information." KARMELO ANTHONY ISOLATED IN JAIL AS TRACK MEET KILLER APPEALS CONVICTION, PREPS FOR PRISON STINT In effect, the filing functioned as a placeholder, preserving prosecutors' ability to ask the judge to admit the evidence later if they believed it became relevant during trial. Filing the notice did not mean the judge would allow jurors to hear it, nor did it mean prosecutors would ultimately decide to offer every allegation listed in the document. That also helps explain why Anthony's filing stretched to 75 pages. CONVICTED KILLER KARMELO ANTHONY SENTENCED TO 35 YEARS AFTER YEARLONG LEGAL BATTLE: TIMELINE Rule 404(b) generally prohibits prosecutors from introducing prior acts simply to argue a defendant has a bad character. But judges may admit that evidence for other purposes if it satisfies the rules of evidence. "When I was a prosecutor, I would put everything but the kitchen sink in the notice," Burks said. "If you don't give the other side notice of it, then you're not going to be able to utilize it later." AUSTIN METCALF'S FATHER HAUNTED BY KARMELO ANTHONY TRIAL VISUALS RELEASED: ‘I HAD NEVER SEEN THOSE PICTURES’ The filing reaches back to Anthony's school years in Louisiana and includes allegations of repeated fights, school suspensions, threats, assaults and misconduct. It also cites text messages in which Anthony allegedly wrote, "When I get mad i see red," "When I get mad i blackout" and "When I get mad i cant control myself." After reviewing the filing following the trial, Metcalf's father, Jeff Metcalf, said he had "no idea" many of the allegations existed until he read the 75-page notice. Speaking with Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno, Metcalf said he was surprised by the scope of the filing. Prosecutors also included photographs and videos they said showed Anthony with what appeared to be firearms, along with messages discussing shootings, robberies and narcotics. The notice itself, however, is not evidence that those alleged acts occurred. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Instead, prosecutors identified them as evidence they said they might ask the court to admit at trial. The filing also cautions that some of the screenshots reflect only portions of larger text conversations. Burks said prior alleged conduct can become especially important when a defendant argues self-defense because prosecutors often try to show the defendant – not the alleged victim – was actually the first aggressor. Rather than trying to prove someone has a violent character, prosecutors may argue prior conduct helps explain who started the confrontation, intent or another issue permitted under Rule 404(b). "The prosecution can file a 404(b) notice to provide some information that can show that the defendant was, in fact, the first aggressor in the situation by showing information of previous aggressive acts," Burks said. "They can also use it to rebut a defensive theory." SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Anthony argued he acted in self-defense when he fatally stabbed Metcalf during an altercation at a Frisco track meet. Prosecutors filed the 404(b) notice roughly a month before trial, preserving the ability to ask the judge to admit dozens of alleged prior acts if they later became relevant during trial. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE The Collin County jury ultimately rejected Anthony's self-defense claim. Instead, the jury convicted him of murder and sentenced him to 35 years in prison after hearing testimony from more than 20 witnesses and reviewing surveillance video from the track meet. SEND US A TIP Whether jurors ultimately hear that evidence, Burks said, is a separate question. GOT A TIP? A judge must first decide whether each item is admissible under the rules of evidence before it can be presented in court. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Burks said many people mistakenly assume a lengthy Rule 404(b) filing means every allegation inside it will eventually be placed before a jury. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "I think probably the biggest misconception people have about 404(b) is they think that because you've given the other side notice of it, that it's automatically going to come in," Burks said. "That is not what it means." articles.title: Pickle-flavored snacks boom as sales jump 30% and craze hits new extremes
articles.summary: Gen Z's social media obsession is fueling pickle mania, from pickle pizza to fried pickle tacos, generating over 80 million engagements in 12 months.
articles.body: America's snack aisle is in a pickle. From chips and crackers to nuts, popcorn and pretzels, pickle flavor is popping up just about everywhere. Pickle-flavored snacks grew 30% in sales over the past year, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing data from market research firm Circana. GEN Z TURNS ON CLASSIC SNACKS, FORCING MAJOR GROCERY SHAKE-UP: 'THEY DON'T TRUST THEM' Beyond snacks, pickle flavor has expanded to smoothies, cheese spreads, hummus — even pickle toothpaste — and it's just getting started, a food and beverage trend expert told Fox News Digital. "According to Datassential's Menu Trends platform, pickles appear on 46% of U.S. restaurant menus, growing 6% over the past four years," said Renee Lee Wege, trendologist and senior publications manager at market research firm Datassential. "That doesn't seem like a lot, but for something already ubiquitous like pickles, that's notable, as it gets into formats like pickle pizza, pickle beverages, etc.," she told Fox News Digital. "We also predict an additional 5% growth on menus in the next four years." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Traditional pickles are most popular among millennials, but younger generations are driving the quirkier flavor applications, Datassential data shows. Forty-eight percent of millennials love pickles, while 76% of this demographic loves or likes them. Gen Z trails in fourth place behind Gen X and boomers, though Wege noted, "that is pickle in general, which is tried-and-true, but pickle-flavored items, especially if they are unique or out there, would likely not be as appealing to older generations." "Where Gen Z plays in is with the unique pickle-flavored items and creations that have been trending on social media, and we all know Gen Z's love affair with social media," she said. Pickle flavor is being propelled by social media virality, Wege noted. "Right now, I think we're in the upper echelon of pickle-mania." "From our social listening data, we see that pickles and pickle-flavored items generated more than 80,880,000 social-media engagements over the past 12 months," she said. "And recent chain examples include Smoothie King's Grillo's Pickles Smoothie, Del Taco's Fried Pickle Taco and McDonald's Dill Pickle McShaker Fries." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Pickle dip is another buzzy social media item, and coming soon to a pizzeria near you: pickle pizza. "In Datassential's 2026 pizza trend data, pickle-related toppings are among the fastest-growing vegetable ingredients on pizza menus, with dill pickle up 73% and pickle up 46% over four years, indicating meaningful recent momentum for pickle pizza components," Wege said. Pickles are ubiquitous and appeal to most consumers, Wege said, but what makes the current craze so pronounced is social media's ability to stir a frenzy around limited-edition offerings, combined with other trends. "This is an evolution of 'maxxing' and consumers, particularly younger ones, looking for 'more is more' and maximalism," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Recent social listening data shows consumers are highly motivated by stronger, more distinctive flavor, with commentary around cane sugar emphasizing enhanced taste and flavor; this helps explain why bold, tangy pickle flavor resonates in the current environment." Has America reached peak pickle? CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Right now, I think we're in the upper echelon of pickle-mania," Wege said, "where the draw is more to 'what else could it do?' or 'make it even crazier and more jaw-dropping,' where the intent is to keep going bigger and weirder and more unique to get attention on social media and make it so consumers have no choice but to try it."

articles.title: China ‘wiretapped Red Sea’ with spy hub 6 miles from US base: ex Pentagon official warns
articles.summary: China's upgraded base near Camp Lemonnier features new antennas and signals intelligence assets turning the Red Sea into a surveillance hub.
articles.body: Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a dangerous surveillance hub, a former Pentagon official warned Sunday, after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint just six miles from a key $66 million-a-year U.S. military base in Djibouti, Africa. The report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) cited new facilities which it said would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it also clarified it was not possible to determine whether China was actively intercepting communications. The developments, one defense expert told Fox News Digital, could also inject fresh tension into U.S.-China relations in the run-up to Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Sept. 24. Beijing's intelligence-gathering capabilities are already under renewed scrutiny. "What China is clearly doing is building eavesdropping capabilities. That seems to be their aim," said Morgan Murphy, former Trump White House official and press secretary for Mark Esper when he was secretary of defense during the first Trump administration. CHINA-LINKED SPY SITE EXPANSION IN CUBA RAISES ALARMS NEAR KEY US MILITARY BASES "Beijing has clearly wiretapped the Red Sea. When you build a 30-meter (100-foot-wide) satellite dish and cover it with a dome, so nobody can see where it's pointing, it's pretty clear you're up to no good," Murphy added while stating of the Washington-based think tank, that "the specificity here reflects the thorough research we expect out of CSIS." The report pinpoints a large southeastern facility showing a control building, three 30-meter dipole antennas for high-frequency communications, two smaller antennas for very and "ultra-high frequencies," three mobile satellite dishes, four probable 5G towers and what CSIS said was a "radome" covering an unidentified asset. CSIS also highlighted two new communications facilities that it says have emerged since 2024 that are likely to form part of a C4ISR command architecture, expanding China’s ability to intercept signals, track naval movements and communicate with Beijing while monitoring foreign militaries in the region. The facilities would provide China with "a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region," the report said. CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES "This isn’t a supply depot — it’s a 50-yard line seat over America’s power projection and the U.S. Navy," Murphy said before stating that the U.S. has "128 bases in more than 51 countries — China has just one." "But look at the location — a few miles from Camp Lemonnier, overlooking the choke point that moves roughly a sixth of global sea trade. Great powers don’t plant listening posts next to rival fleets for 'logistics,'" he warned. "Britain held Gibraltar to see who entered the Med while Japan’s island radios came before the runways. The Soviets’ overseas sites were never just about fuel and Beijing is running that playbook on the Red Sea," Murphy added. Although China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jian said China is "unaware of the specific situation" and framed the country as a "builder of international peace," the new facilities provide Beijing with a picture of regional operations, according to Reuters. CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE "The new report is helpful in framing the conversation, and it comes at an awkward time for China because Xi Jinping is visiting the White House on the 24th of this month," Murphy said. "I'd bet a box of donuts this issue comes up. There is going to be public exposure of this, which Chinese leadership isn't used to. They aren't used to being asked tough questions by the press," he said. President Donald Trump recently addressed Chinese intelligence efforts aboard Air Force One, acknowledging that China "spies on us" just as "we spy on them." Trump's comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal linking support from a Chinese entity to high-resolution satellite imagery used by Iran prior to a deadly missile attack on U.S. troops in Jordan. "They basically do what we do," Trump noted, adding that "Xi has behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well. ... You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you're right, and we spy on them, too," he said, according to Reuters. RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER Murphy noted, "Nations spy on each other — allies and adversaries alike." "It is a very old playbook, and listening posts all over the world are typical of great powers, but where the metal hits the floorboard is when you try to use that information," he said before adding that China may "keep tabs on us, but they cannot project power like the United States can." The proximity of China's facility to U.S. operations is a core concern. Located less than six miles from Camp Lemonnier — the primary U.S. counterterrorism hub in Africa — and near French, Italian and Japanese installations, the site has a history of friction with U.S. forces. "We are just right around the corner from China, and yet it's not a cooperative relationship," Murphy explained. "Back in 2018, they lasered two of our C-130 pilots' eyes who suffered lasting damage from that incident. Beijing denied it, of course, but we know the truth." WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA During the 2018 incident, the Pentagon had formally complained to China after military-grade lasers were pointed at American pilots attempting to land at Camp Lemonnier, causing minor injuries. While Beijing dismissed the allegations as "groundless accusations," the confrontation underscored the potential for friction between military forces operating from nearby bases. "China has one overseas base. The United States has more than 128 — by some counts, over 700 installations around the world," Murphy said. "So it's significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from ours in Djibouti. It is hugely strategically important, which is why, of course, we're there." IS TRUMP CONSIDERING BOLD AFRICA PLAY TO PUSH BACK ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND ISLAMIC TERRORISTS? "It's our only base on the continent of Africa," he said, noting that it shares a "parking lot" with Japanese and Italian bases. "At $66 million a year, it's the best money Americans spend on our defense budget, full stop." The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a choke point for nearly 16% of global maritime trade and, with significant crude shipments, Houthi attacks and pipeline disruptions have fueled a regional military buildup. "Interference by China is in their strategic interest. They don't want to see the United States able to control their oil supply," Murphy said. "China is far more reliant on Middle Eastern oil than the United States. China imports a huge portion — around 33% or more — of their daily oil needs and is highly reliant on long sea lines. You are seeing this muscle-flexing because they are far more reliant on Middle Eastern oil than we are." TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA "Having intelligence is one thing, but you must have the ability to act on it. You need assets in the region," Murphy said. "China doesn't have major combat assets outside their region because they lack a blue-water navy to project power outside the first island chain yet. "That is coming, and they are working towards it quickly. Americans can take comfort in the fact that they don't have that capacity today, but we must stay alert because the only thing that subdues a threat is a ready posture," he concluded. articles.title: A simple guide to the Yemen conflict
articles.summary: Here’s a brief history of Yemen’s war – from the Houthi takeover in 2014 to the latest escalation.
articles.body:
Yemen is back in the global spotlight after the Iran-aligned Houthi group earlier this month made military gains against the forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, tightening its grip over the Red Sea coast.

The latest escalation in the Arab region’s most impoverished nation follows a period of relative calm that had largely held since the United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022 between the Iran-aligned group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

The Houthi takeover of northwestern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, in 2014 had drawn Saudi military intervention. The fighting left tens of thousands dead and millions displaced, creating a humanitarian crisis.

In 2023, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis agreed to a UN roadmap towards a permanent ceasefire after direct talks, but the roadmap was never formalised.

Here’s a simple guide to Yemen’s war, from the Houthi takeover in 2014 to the latest escalation .

From the 2014 Houthi takeover to the expansion of the Saudi-backed government

The Houthis took over vast swaths of northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, and months later assumed control of the government, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee to Aden and then to Saudi Arabia.

Alarmed by the rise of the Iran-aligned Houthis on its border, Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government of Hadi in March 2015, carrying out thousands of attacks. Saudi Arabia sees Iran as a regional threat due to the latter’s financial and military power, as well as support for armed groups like Hezbollah.

In this period, Houthi rebels targeted strategic infrastructure across Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), including airports, gas fields and oil tankers in the Red Sea. According to data analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Saudi Arabia’s military intercepted more than 4,000 Houthi missiles, drones and other standoff weapons between 2017 and 2022.

In 2019, the UN reported that about 24 million people (80 percent of the population) needed some form of assistance, making Yemen “the world’s worst humanitarian crisis” after nearly five years of war. The country also experienced the world’s worst cholera outbreak, amid the war‑damaged health and water systems. Millions of people were exposed, and hundreds of thousands of suspected cases were recorded.

After seven years of conflict, the UN-mediated truce took effect in April 2022, bringing a marked de-escalation in fighting, even while a low-intensity conflict had remained since.

In January of this year, Yemen’s internationally recognised government expanded its control of the southern and eastern parts of the country after the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) announced its dissolution .

The UAE’s backing of the STC, which called for the secession and independence of southern Yemen, strained Saudi-UAE ties, with Riyadh asking the Emirati forces to leave the country.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), are an armed group in control of mainly northwestern Yemen and several areas close to Saudi Arabia. Since September 10, they have tightened control over the country’s Red Sea coast, a vital shipping lane.

The Houthis from Yemen’s Zaidi Shia minority emerged in the northern mountainous region of Saada in the 1990s, demanding a greater share of power.

They capitalised on the widespread public anger against the weak transitional government that came to power after longtime President Ali Abdullah Saleh was forced to step down following the 2011 Arab Spring protests.

The Houthis initially allied with military units loyal to former President Saleh as they captured the Red Sea port of Hodeidah in October 2014. In January 2015, they seized the presidential palace in Sanaa, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee to the southern port city of Aden. Hadi later moved to Saudi Arabia, from where he ran his government-in-exile until his resignation in 2022.

The Houthi group then spent years, with Iran’s backing, fighting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia.

Seen as part of a regional alliance known as the “axis of resistance” and backed by Iran, the Houthi group nevertheless has its own base, its own interests, and its own ambitions.

The group has gained international prominence for its attacks on Israel and shipping in the Red Sea since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza in October 2023.

Riyadh entered the Yemen war when it led a military coalition against the Houthis in March 2015, seeking to restore the government of then-President Hadi.

Houthis have accused Riyadh of carrying out hundreds of attacks in support of the internationally recognised government battling the Houthis in the latest fighting.

The PLC was established in 2022 when former President Hadi formally transferred his powers to the new eight-member body.

It represents the internationally recognised government of Yemen, with a mandate to manage the country’s political, security and military affairs, and to steer negotiations towards a permanent ceasefire. It is chaired by Rashad al-Alimi, an adviser to Hadi and former interior minister with the government of the late President Saleh.

Its membership is drawn from a mix of northern and southern politicians and military-linked leaders in a bid to unite major anti-Houthi forces under one roof.

The PLC is backed by Saudi Arabia and the alliance that Riyadh leads. Since taking over complete control of southern Yemen after the dissolution of the STC, the PLC aims to unite Yemen, including the areas controlled by the Houthis.

The Yemeni Congregation for Reform, better known as Islah, is a Sunni Islamist movement with historical ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. It is a faction within the recognised PLC-led government but has long had an independent identity. Its major stronghold has long been Marib, the country’s sole gas-producing region with one of its largest oilfields.

The National Resistance Forces is a government-aligned military faction led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late former President Saleh.

The force has maintained ties to Saudi Arabia and, like the Islah party, is part of the PLC. It aims for a unified Yemen, positioning itself as a counterweight to both the Houthis and southern secessionists.

The Houthi movement controls Sanaa, the capital, and most of northwestern and northern Yemen, including the entire Red Sea coastline and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the busiest global maritime routes. The control over Bab al-Mandeb by the Iran-aligned Houthis has raised concerns about navigation amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran in response to the US-Israel war on Tehran.

The internationally recognised government, meanwhile, controls much of the rest of the country.

More than 112,000 people have been displaced in Yemen and close to 3,000 have fled the conflict to Djibouti, according to the UN.

The International Organization for Migration estimated that 22 million Yemenis, nearly half the population, are in urgent need of humanitarian aid.

The UN Security Council, meanwhile, has condemned the Houthis’ continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they have caused civilian casualties, including women and children, and damaged energy infrastructure.

What do we know about the latest fighting?

Tensions escalated in July after Yemen’s government forces claimed an attack on an airport in Sanaa, preventing an aircraft from Iran from landing. More attacks followed, and it further escalated in late August when the Houthis launched a major offensive, saying the 2022 truce had been violated by government forces.

The Saudi Arabia-led coalition on Saturday evening said on X that it “successfully intercepted and destroyed” a missile attack attempting to target Riyadh – the first attack on the capital since the Yemen conflict erupted in July.

The coalition added that the Houthis had tried to target “civilians and civilian infrastructure” in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil, which were additionally thwarted.

The Houthis confirmed they had targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh, as well as Aramco facilities in Yanbu.

“The message from the Yemeni group is that despite the Saudi bombardment campaign across Yemen, it will continue to step up its attacks and meet escalation with escalation,” said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa.

The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a “cowardly terrorist attack” on Islam’s holy city. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a “worn-out lie”.

Meanwhile, on the ground in Yemen, the armed forces of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government and the Houthis are engaged in fierce fighting in southern Marib as well as Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and al-Bayda.

The Yemeni army also said 13 soldiers were killed in two days of clashes with Houthi forces in the southwestern provinces of Taiz and Lahj.

On September 10, the Houthis made their most crucial gain in this bout of fighting by seizing the crucial Red Sea city of Mocha, expanding control over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Despite appeals from Riyadh for United States President Donald Trump to strike the Houthis directly, Washington has so far held back, wary of opening a new front while still fighting a costly war with Iran.

Meanwhile, US officials have met Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend. The Houthis reportedly assured Washington that vessels not linked to Saudi Arabia would not be targeted.

The Houthis have banned the passage of Saudi ships, adding pressure on Riyadh, which has used the Red Sea as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis also attacked the East-West pipeline, disrupting the export of Saudi oil and causing global oil prices to cross $100 per barrel.

(Al Jazeera)

articles.title: Dak Prescott gave more than $1 million to his Louisiana high school, funding a huge new video board and revamped weight room
articles.summary: US News: Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott gifted more than $1 million to his alma mater, Haughton High School in Haughton, Louisiana, funding a new vide.
articles.body: Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott gifted more than $1 million to his alma mater, Haughton High School in Haughton, Louisiana, funding a new video scoreboard, described as one of the largest of its kind in the state, and a revamped weight room. The gift was honoured at a ceremony on 5 November 2025, where the school's football field was dedicated as Prescott Field. Here's how the donation came together, and what the ceremony meant to the community that watched him grow up.Dak Prescott's $1 million gift to his alma mater, Haughton High SchoolAhead of the 2025 football season, Prescott gifted more than $1 million to Haughton High School, as per KTBS, funding what was the largest video scoreboard of its kind in Louisiana, along with a revamped weight room. In the same space, he once trained alongside his own teammates. As KSLA News 12 reported, a ceremony honouring the donation was held on 5 November 2025 at 6 p.m., during which the school's football field was officially dedicated as Prescott Field.The Prescott Field dedication ceremonyThe dedication was held at Harlan Stadium and doubled as a fundraiser for Haughton Athletics, with tickets priced at $5 and free admission for Bossier Parish School Board employees with an ID badge. The event drew a large crowd, complete with fireworks and applause, welcoming Prescott back to the same stadium where his high school career began. Reflecting on the moment, Prescott told KTBS 3 the day was something he had once imagined for himself and his brothers, thanking Haughton for the occasion.Prescott's history of giving back to HaughtonSince beginning his NFL career, Prescott has remained closely connected to his former school. Beyond the scoreboard and weight room donation, his philanthropy has included hosting youth football camps, donating sports equipment and uniforms, purchasing school supplies, and sponsoring athletic events at Haughton, a pattern the outlet reported has spanned several years, citing a school news release.Prescott's record-setting career and ties to HaughtonAccording to KTAL/KMSS, Prescott last played for Haughton in 2010, leading the team to the only undefeated regular season in the school's history. He still holds several school records, including career passing touchdowns (80) and rushing touchdowns (37), as well as passing touchdowns in a single season (39). At the dedication, Prescott told KTAL News he was proud to be "from Haughton" and to call himself a Buccaneer, underscoring the lasting bond between the NFL quarterback and the small Bossier Parish town where his football career first began.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: North Korea defends overseas labor program, rejecting sanctions report
articles.summary: North Korea said Monday that it would not tolerate what it called hostile forces’ efforts to curb Pyongyang’s cooperation with other countries, adding that no new sanctions would block its development or defense of its core interests.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea said Monday that it would not tolerate what it called hostile forces’ efforts to curb Pyongyang’s cooperation with other countries, adding that no new sanctions would block its development or defense of its core interests, state news agency KCNA reported, citing a Foreign Ministry spokesperson. The statement accused the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), a group of 11 U.N. members that tracks and reports violations and evasion of sanctions, of fabricating a report aimed at portraying what North Korea described as normal, mutually beneficial economic cooperation between itself and other countries as illegal, KCNA said. The MSMT said in a report issued Sept. 16 that North Korea continued to send laborers overseas in breach of U.N. Security Council resolutions, generating an estimated $450 million to $800 million in 2025 to fund its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs. It estimated that 35,600 to 101,280 North Korean workers remain active in at least 17 countries, mainly China and Russia, and called for countries to immediately enforce U.N. resolutions by repatriating North Korean workers and refusing new work permits. MSMT participating states include Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States, the report said.

articles.title: Former husband and in-laws of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi stand trial in her killing
articles.summary: A murder trial began Monday for the former husband and in-laws of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi more than three years after the discovery of parts of her dismembered body at a house shocked the city where violent crime is rare.
articles.body: HONG KONG — A murder trial began Monday for the former husband and in-laws of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi more than three years after the discovery of parts of her dismembered body at a house shocked the Chinese territory, where violent crime is rare. Choi’s ex-husband Alex Kwong, his father Kwong Kau and his brother Anthony Kwong were accused of killing Choi in February 2023. They face life imprisonment if convicted of murder. They were also charged with preventing the lawful burial of a body. Choi was a 28-year-old socialite who shared her glamorous life of photo shoots and fashion shows on Instagram. Days before her death, she posted about attending a Dior show at Paris Fashion Week. Choi’s killing transfixed many in the Asian financial hub, which has a very low level of violent crime. Dozens of people waited outside the courtroom for the hearing to start, and a live broadcast was arranged for people to watch outside it. All three defendants wore masks and appeared calm in court. Kwong Kau was in a white T-shirt, while his sons wore suits. Police said in 2023 that they found some body parts inside the unit at a village in Tai Po, a suburban district in Hong Kong. Officers later searched a landfill for evidence. Choi had two children with Alex Kwong. She remarried after their divorce and had two younger children with her second husband. The prosecution is expected to open its case at a later date. The jury trial is expected to last 45 days.

articles.title: How oil, gas losses have shrunk Iran’s GDP by 10 percent during war
articles.summary: The oil and gas sector shrank 26 percent, new official data shows, pointing to the costs of the US-Israel war on Iran.
articles.body:
Amid the US-Israel war on Iran, the country’s economy has suffered a sharp contraction, with its crucial oil and gas sector taking the biggest hit as the United States tightens its economic and military pressure on Tehran.

Data released by the government-administered Statistical Center of Iran showed gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar.

The period covers the opening months of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.

The economic downturn has come as Iran struggles to export its oil, one of its most important sources of foreign currency, while also contending with high inflation, a weakening rial, and disruptions to trade and industry.

The headline GDP number masks an even steeper decline in Iran’s energy industry. Crude oil and natural gas activity contracted by 26.4 percent compared with the same period a year earlier. GDP excluding oil, by comparison, fell by 4.6 percent.

The damage has spread beyond the energy sector. Industry and mining contracted by 14.7 percent, services declined by 4.8 percent, and manufacturing contracted by 2.5 percent. Agriculture was the exception, growing at 2.3 percent.

Those figures come amid an already difficult economic situation in the country. Earlier this month, Iran’s 12-month average inflation reached 69.9 percent, while food, beverage, and tobacco prices rose at nearly twice that rate. Official unemployment climbed to 9.1 percent in the spring.

The rial, meanwhile, fell from about one million to the US dollar a year earlier to more than 2.2 million in early September.

What is the latest with Iran’s oil exports?

Iran’s ability to sell crude has been dramatically curtailed by the US naval blockade, imposed for most of the war.

Iranian crude and condensate loadings collapsed from about two million barrels per day in March to roughly 740,000bpd in July and just 220,000-255,000bpd in August, according to estimates from Kpler and Vortexa.

TankerTrackers.com told the Reuters news agency that 29 tankers, carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, were trapped in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Vortexa estimated total Iranian crude afloat had fallen from 135 million barrels at the end of July to 107 million barrels by late August.

Is Trump winning the economic war on Iran?

By several economic measures, Washington’s pressure campaign is inflicting damage on Iran’s economy.

On September 6, total trade had fallen by 25 to 35 percent, President Masoud Pezeshkian said, with imports hit harder than exports. The US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has made it hard for ships carrying imports to reach Iranian ports.

Tehran has also explicitly linked the end of the war to economic relief. Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera on Saturday that its conditions include “the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade”.

In addition to the naval blockade, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last month announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, pledging to target its financial interests across the world. He said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran.

The US-Israeli attacks and Iran’s retaliations have disrupted Tehran’s trade with one of its main economic partners, the United Arab Emirates.

The UAE last month announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran after accusing its forces of carrying out several ballistic missile attacks, which Tehran denied, calling it a “false flag operation” by Israel and the US.

Chris Beauchamp, market analyst at IG Group, said, “Most wars are contests of stamina more than anything else.”

“The 10 percent drop in Iranian GDP is a sign that the US is succeeding in putting pressure on its foe. But the question rests, as it has done since March, on whether Iran can weather the fall in economic activity better than the US can stand the surge in energy costs,” he told Al Jazeera.

“For a regime prepared to do anything to stay in power, this news will make little difference, so long as the security forces remain loyal,” he added.

What is the latest with diplomatic efforts to end the war?

While Iran has taken a defiant stance against US economic and military pressure, it has indicated repeatedly that it remains open to diplomatic means to end the nearly seven-month-old war.

On Saturday, Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran conveyed a formal set of conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators for ending the war.

Iranian state media outlet IRNA reported on Monday that Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi was set to visit Tehran, without specifying the agenda or other details.

Mediators Qatar and Pakistan have been working to re-establish negotiations between the two sides since their memorandum of understanding (MoU) expired last month.

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will stop briefly in Qatar before going to New York for the UN General Assembly, IRNA reported.

Iran has repeatedly said it remains ready for any new strikes by Washington.

Rezaei said on Saturday Tehran did not rule out a new US strike against Iran, calling the possibility “very much on the cards” based on his country’s military assessments.

Mark Pfeifle, a Republican strategist and former White House and national security official, said Iran and the US are still willing to strike a deal.

“Sometimes in diplomacy it’s what’s taken off the table,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pfeifle said when Rezaei reiterated his demands for talks with the US, he spoke of “ending the blockade, releasing the frozen funds [and] stopping the attacks”.

“But he left off reparations and reconstruction money, which tells me that there’s a concrete sign that amongst all the rhetoric, which is still very strident, that the pressure campaign that the US is putting on Iran is having some effect,” he said.

“And it tells me that both sides are still looking for room to negotiate in the coming weeks.”
