articles.title: In 1905, Beatrix Potter bought a 34-acre Lake District farm with royalties from Peter Rabbit; it soon had sheep, cows, pigs, ducks and hens
articles.summary: UK News: Beatrix Potter used the success of The Tale of Peter Rabbit to buy Hill Top, a 17th-century farmhouse and 34-acre farm in the Lake District village of.
articles.body: Beatrix Potter used the success of The Tale of Peter Rabbit to buy Hill Top, a 17th-century farmhouse and 34-acre farm in the Lake District village of Near Sawrey, in 1905. Potter was 39 and had already published six books with Frederick Warne & Co when she bought the property with proceeds from Peter Rabbit and a small inheritance from an aunt. Although she could not live there permanently at first because she was expected to spend much of the year with her parents in London, Hill Top quickly became both a working farm and a source of inspiration for her writing. She hired a property manager and began learning about Lakeland farming, eventually developing a particular commitment to Herdwick sheep. Over the following decades, her interests shifted increasingly from writing towards farming, land management and conservation, and by the time of her death in 1943, she had built up a substantial estate that she left to the National Trust.The farm gave Beatrix Potter a new kind of independenceHill Top represented something very different from Potter's life in London. She had spent many summers in the Lake District from childhood and regarded the countryside as a place where she could work and pursue her interests away from the restrictions of her family's London life. The National Trust describes Hill Top as a refuge that became a place of independence and inspiration. Margaret Lane, in her 1968 biography of Potter, described the farm as a symbol of freedom to its owner.The purchase also came during a period of personal upheaval. In 1905, Potter became engaged to Norman Warne, her editor at Frederick Warne & Co. Warne died suddenly just four weeks after proposing. Potter responded by throwing herself into her work and continued producing the children's books that had begun to make her successful. The National Trust says she also threw herself into running Hill Top while continuing to work on more of her “little books”.Hill Top became part of her storiesThe landscape around Near Sawrey became closely connected with Potter's writing. The National Trust says the area around Sawrey and nearby Hawkshead provided settings for nine of her little books. The Tale of Jeremy Fisher, published in 1906, was set on nearby Esthwaite Water, while the garden and house at Hill Top can be recognised in The Tale of Tom Kitten, published in 1907. The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, published in 1908, drew directly from Potter's life at the farm. According to the National Trust, the story was based on a real runaway duck at Hill Top. Potter's surroundings were therefore not simply a backdrop for her illustrations. Animals, buildings, gardens and the wider landscape became material for the stories themselves. After marrying solicitor William Heelis in 1913, Potter moved into Castle Cottage, while Hill Top remained an important place for her writing and creative work. At the same time, her involvement in farming continued to deepen.Farming gradually became central to her lifePotter was a lifelong learner when it came to Lakeland farming. She worked closely with experienced farmers and shepherds and became particularly committed to breeding Herdwick sheep, a native Lakeland breed. Her correspondence shows how closely she involved herself in the day-to-day management of her land and livestock. A 1916 letter to Eleanor Choyce, a farmhand Potter employed during the First World War, gives an unusually detailed picture of Hill Top. Potter described the farm as covering 120 acres, including 9 acres of arable land, with 2 horses, 9 or 10 cows and 60 sheep, 47 of them lambing ewes. She also mentioned poultry, an orchard, a flower garden and vegetables, as well as the Cannon family, who had worked on the farm for years.The change in Potter's identity is visible in official records. The 1911 census recorded her occupation as “authoress”. By the 1921 census, after her marriage to Heelis, there was no mention of her earlier profession and she was recorded simply as a “farmer”. The National Trust's Assistant National Curator Helen Antrobus describes this as evidence of how deeply Potter had committed herself to managing her farms.Her farming empire eventually stretched across the Lake DistrictHill Top was only the beginning. Potter continued buying farms and land in the Lake District, developing large flocks of Herdwick sheep and working with experienced local farmers. After purchasing Troutbeck Park Farm in 1923, she was managing more than 1,000 Herdwick sheep across more than 1,800 acres. Her head shepherd, Tom Storey, helped improve the condition of the Troutbeck flock, and after moving to Hill Top in 1927, he helped establish a highly regarded Herdwick flock there. Potter's sheep went on to win awards at local agricultural shows.Farming was not simply a source of income for Potter. She continued to write about the difficulties of falling wool prices, including in a December 1930 letter in which she complained that the price of wool had dropped sharply. At the same time, her involvement with the land increasingly extended into conservation. She worked with the National Trust and supported efforts to protect the Lake District from inappropriate development, using money from her books and land purchases to help preserve parts of the landscape she valued. When Potter died in 1943, she left around 4,000 acres of land and 15 farms, along with flocks of Herdwick sheep, to the National Trust. She stipulated that Hill Top, her most treasured home, should be preserved as she had left it. The farmhouse remains in the Trust's care, while Hill Top Farm continues to operate as a working farm with Herdwick sheep descended from Potter's original flock.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Alexander Dennis Scarborough strike over after pay deal - union
articles.summary: About 400 workers in Scarborough began industrial action in June but have now returned, union says.
articles.body:
Hundreds of workers at a bus manufacturer have ended strike action after securing an above-inflation pay deal.

About 400 staff members in the Unite union at Alexander Dennis in Scarborough had walked out in June after rejecting management's offer of a 4% increase. Nationally, CPI inflation was 3.1% in the year to August 2026.

The workers have now accepted a 4.5% rise, back-dated to January, with a further 3.5% increase in January 2027, the union said.

A spokesperson for Alexander Dennis said an agreement had been reached that "enables us to resume full manufacturing operations at our Scarborough site and continue to deliver for our customers".

Formed 130 years ago, the firm produces buses for Greater Manchester's Bee Network and also Transport for London.

The company, which is headquartered in Larbert, Scotland, was also recently awarded a contract to build more than 200 buses for the Liverpool City Region.

Unite's regional officer Dan Stephens said workers were now "focused on getting back to proudly building world-class buses".

A spokesperson for Alexander Dennis said that Prime Minister Andy Burnham and metro mayors had spoken about the importance of the UK bus manufacturing sector.

"It is essential that those ambitions are reflected in procurement decisions that sustain skilled jobs, create more apprenticeships and deliver economic growth across the country," they added.

articles.title: Flying taxis are taking off in Texas. Is your city next?
articles.summary: Joby Aviation flew its eVTOL air taxi into DFW Airport's busy airspace as Texas launches Project Nexus, a three-year advanced air mobility program.
articles.body: If you have ever watched your arrival time creep later while sitting in traffic, flying over it sounds pretty appealing. Texas is now testing what that could look like. Earlier this month, the Texas Department of Transportation launched the first phase of Project Nexus, a three-year program focused on preparing next-generation aircraft for use in Texas skies. The Sept. 10 kickoff at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport included demonstrations from BETA Technologies and Joby Aviation. Joby brought its electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as an eVTOL. No passengers climbed aboard the initial Project Nexus flights. Instead, Texas is starting to learn how air taxis could eventually fit into the way people get around. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE Flying taxi testing has officially started in Texas Project Nexus will advance in phases over the next three years. The broader first phase uses traditional aircraft, including helicopters and fixed-wing planes, to test routes and collect data. TxDOT says those initial flights will help validate routes and prepare for future advanced air mobility operations. Joby also launched a week-long campaign of piloted electric air taxi flights across North Texas under TxDOT's Project Nexus proposal, part of the federal eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The campaign included planned direct flights into DFW International Airport, a round trip to Arlington and a route connecting Alliance Airport with Toyota Motor North America's headquarters in Plano. One of the biggest tests involved DFW. Joby's campaign called for a direct flight into DFW's controlled airspace, with the aircraft landing at DFW Corporate Aviation. That puts an eVTOL into the same busy airspace used by one of the world's busiest airports. That kind of testing can tell regulators much more about how these aircraft might eventually operate around major transportation hubs. Air taxis are getting closer to reality We have been following electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as eVTOLs, for years. They can rise vertically like a helicopter. Many designs then transition into forward flight using wings. Earlier this year, we looked at how a federal pilot program could bring air taxis into U.S. skies before the industry reaches full commercial service. We have also covered plans for air taxis serving New York City's three major airports and Joby's partnership with Virgin Atlantic to develop electric air taxi service in the United Kingdom. So the aircraft themselves are no longer the biggest surprise. What gets my attention now is where companies are flying them and how regulators are testing their ability to operate around airports people already use. That's where Project Nexus comes in. Why Dallas-Fort Worth gives air taxis a serious test Flying around Dallas-Fort Worth creates challenges you do not get at an isolated test site. Joby's campaign included planned missions between Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport and several destinations around the region. DFW International Airport was part of that schedule. The company and federal researchers have been preparing for this type of operation for years. Joby says the FAA and NASA began studying electric air taxi integration in North Texas in 2018. Then, in 2023, Joby and NASA ran a detailed simulation examining whether the DFW terminal area could handle as many as 50 electric air taxi operations per hour. Now that work is moving from computer simulations to aircraft operating in North Texas. Joby has also leased a 45,000-square-foot facility at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport. The new facility gives Joby a long-term operating presence in North Texas, well beyond this initial flight campaign. AI AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM PROMISES FEWER FLIGHT DELAYS Project Nexus may move medical supplies before passengers Here's where the Texas plan gets especially interesting. Air taxis tend to grab attention because people imagine hopping aboard and flying over traffic. But some early Project Nexus missions could have nothing to do with your commute. Later phases are expected to focus on medical and cargo logistics. TxDOT specifically points to transporting critical medical supplies or organs between rural facilities and urban medical centers in Austin and San Antonio. That's a use case that could be easier to understand than flying across town to save a few minutes. Moving time-sensitive medical supplies faster could show where this technology provides practical value while passenger operations continue developing. Passenger air taxis come later Eventually, Project Nexus plans to put passengers onboard. TxDOT says the final phase will involve passenger air taxi flights across the Texas Triangle. TxDOT's plan calls for regional air taxi connections involving Dallas, Austin, San Antonio and Houston. That does not mean commercial passenger service across Texas has a firm launch date. Joby still has certification work ahead. The company says it has advanced into the fifth and final stage of FAA type certification, with testing continuing as part of that process. So you probably will not see an air taxi button appear beside your rideshare options tomorrow. The work happening now is about figuring out how these aircraft could operate safely before passenger service expands. Air taxi testing is spreading across the US Texas is getting a lot of attention right now, but Project Nexus is part of a much larger federal effort. The eVTOL Integration Pilot Program includes eight projects across 26 states, with testing focused on passenger travel, cargo and medical transportation. We have already seen some of that play out. Earlier this month, we covered the FAA's testing of Elroy Air's pilotless hybrid-electric Chaparral cargo aircraft. BETA Technologies and United Therapeutics have also tested electric aircraft for transporting organs between Virginia and Maryland. Other projects involve New York and New Jersey, Florida and several additional states. So while Texas is one of the biggest air taxi test beds right now, it is far from the only one. That raises the bigger question: If these trials keep expanding, how long will it be before you start seeing aircraft like these closer to home? DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES What this means to you If air taxis eventually come to your area, the big question will be simple: Will they actually make your life easier? Skipping over traffic sounds great, especially on the way to an airport or across a crowded metro area. But the convenience depends on where these aircraft take off and land, how much a ride costs and how much time you really save from door to door. You will also want to know what frequent flights sound like overhead. Electric aircraft are designed to be quieter than helicopters, but there is a big difference between hearing one occasionally and having them fly regularly near your neighborhood. And before any of this becomes routine, the FAA has to be comfortable with the safety side. That's exactly why these Texas tests are important. They give regulators a chance to see how the aircraft handle busy airspace before passenger flights become more common. For me, that is what makes Project Nexus worth watching. We already know these aircraft can fly. Now we are starting to find out whether they can fit into the way we actually travel. Kurt's key takeaways I have been watching air taxis develop for years, but Project Nexus feels like the kind of test that can tell us whether they have a real shot at becoming useful transportation. Flying around North Texas and operating at DFW gives Joby a chance to show how these aircraft can handle the kind of busy airspace they would face in regular service. I am also really interested in the medical side. If an electric aircraft can move an organ or critical supplies faster between hospitals, that could be one of the first places where this technology shows its value. For passengers, though, I still come back to two things: price and convenience. If the landing site is 30 minutes out of your way or the fare costs a fortune, flying over traffic starts to lose some of its appeal. Noise will also be something communities pay close attention to as more of these aircraft take to the sky. We already know air taxis can fly. What I want to see now is whether they can save you enough time, at a price you can live with, to make you actually want to book one. If an air taxi could turn an hour in traffic into a 15-minute flight, how much would you be willing to pay to take it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Converse apologizes and pulls sneaker ad that critics said included racist imagery
articles.summary: The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan and lynching.
articles.body: The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan and lynching. The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers. Critics lashed out online, saying that a white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a KKK hood and that the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim. Converse, owned by Nike, issued a statement apologizing and saying it had removed the ad. “We’re sorry,” said the statement, first released on Friday. “We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better.” Converse, based in Boston, declined on Sunday to answer questions seeking additional information, including how the company screens ads before they are posted and how the ad was approved. Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts. Retailers and top fashion brands have issued a string of apologies over the years for products criticized as being racially insensitive. Last month, retailer Target pulled a children’s Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures. The Converse photo sparked swift criticism, including calls for staff involved in the ad to be fired and for a boycott of the company. In a slew of comments on social media, posters questioned how the ad could have cleared the company’s advertising vetting process. Other commenters defended Converse, saying they didn’t believe it was intentional. Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney based in Texas, posted on Instagram that Converse’s apology “doesn’t undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step.” “We keep having this conversation because corporations keep failing the same test,” he wrote. “Do better means catching this before it airs — not after we’re offended.” Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in 1908, makes the iconic Chuck Taylor All Star sneaker. It was first released in 1917 as a non-skid basketball shoe, adding the signature of Taylor — a basketball player who promoted the sneaker — in 1934, according to the company’s website.

articles.title: 'Will protect out 1st amendment right': CNN, MS NOW & Politico to sue Trump admin over White House ban
articles.summary: US News: CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after journalists are barred from White House, arguing that the move violates their First .
articles.body: CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after journalists are barred from White House, arguing that the move violates their First Amendment rights.The three news organisations notified the administration on Monday that they were taking legal action and asked a federal court in Washington to restore their access. The case could lead to hearings and arguments over the White House's decision as early as this week.The lawsuit follows President Donald Trump's announcement on Friday that the three outlets would be barred from the White House over coverage he described as negative. Trump also indicated that other news organisations could face similar restrictions.Reporters denied White House entryThe restrictions were enforced on Saturday when reporters from the three organisations arrived to cover the administration.CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett were denied entry to the White House grounds and had their press credentials confiscated, according to reports.CNN and MS NOW have also been prevented from using their television equipment and designated camera locations at the White House. CNN was subsequently removed from its scheduled television pool duties, including coverage involving the president's travel.The three organisations said the administration revoked their journalists' credentials without notice or a process for challenging the decision."This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the outlets said in a joint statement.They added that the action threatened press freedom and the public's access to independent journalism.First Amendment disputeAt the centre of the case is whether the government can restrict journalists' access to the White House because of the content or viewpoint of their reporting.The outlets are expected to argue that Trump's stated dissatisfaction with their coverage amounts to viewpoint discrimination. Courts have previously considered restrictions on White House press access in cases involving journalists and news organisations.A 1977 ruling by the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit involved The Nation reporter Robert Sherrill, whose White House press credentials had been revoked. The court held that denying a White House press pass based on the content of a journalist's speech or discriminatory treatment of protected speech could violate the First Amendment, CNN reported.That precedent has featured in later disputes involving White House press access. During Trump's first presidency, CNN reporter Jim Acosta, Playboy correspondent Brian Karem and The Associated Press also faced restrictions on access, with courts siding with journalists in several cases.Ted Boutrous, a First Amendment lawyer who represented CNN during its 2018 legal dispute with the Trump administration over Acosta's access, is representing the three organisations in the latest case.The administration, meanwhile, has pointed to its authority over access to the White House. At least one Trump administration official has argued that a 1965 Supreme Court ruling concerning passport restrictions could support the president's position.The three news organisations have said they will continue covering the Trump administration despite being denied physical access to the White House.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why do Sudan’s humanitarian truces keep failing and who is to blame?
articles.summary: Efforts to bring about humanitarian truces in Sudan hit a dead end as warring factions prioritise battlefield victories.
articles.body:
Efforts to bring about truces in Sudan are continuing to hit a dead end, with fighting continuing and worsening the country’s dire humanitarian situation.

Renewed efforts, including by the United States, to implement temporary truces to allow desperately needed aid into the country have repeatedly failed. Fighting has intensified in recent months, with the United Nations warning that the humanitarian system in Sudan is on the brink of collapse.

Aid groups have urged immediate truces to alleviate the humanitarian crisis, but rival factions continue to maintain their momentum on the battlefield and break local ceasefires.

Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 after months of tensions between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) group. It expanded into 13 out of Sudan’s 18 states and has forcibly displaced 14 million people, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises and killing tens of thousands of people.

Several international mediation efforts have attempted to broker ceasefires to end fighting and bolster humanitarian efforts, amid cases of starvation.

The first major initiative, the Jeddah Declaration in May 2023 , was mediated and guaranteed by the US and Saudi Arabia. While it temporarily facilitated limited humanitarian access to affected communities, it soon collapsed after both factions repeatedly violated the terms.

Regional efforts via the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the African Union (AU) similarly failed when localised, short-term truces broke down, sometimes just hours after they were implemented.

The US has significantly ramped up its diplomatic engagement over the past year, spearheading the Aligned for Advancing Lifesaving and Peace in Sudan (ALPS) initiative in Geneva. Alongside Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the UAE, the UN, and the AU, Washington has pushed for direct negotiations and localised humanitarian pauses.

Responding to the escalating crisis, US Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos last week committed $375m to humanitarian efforts in Sudan and reiterated that “there is no military solution to this conflict.”

The US has reportedly renewed calls for a 90-day humanitarian truce in Sudan and for allowing affected communities to access emergency aid.

Fighting continues on multiple fronts in Sudan. In South Kordofan, the SAF has claimed gains, while Al Jazeera sources reported that the army had repelled an attack by the RSF in Blue Nile state. Conversely, the RSF has claimed a major victory over the army and its allies in Abu Qauod, west of El Obeid. With both sides claiming to be winning, it could make the prospects of a peaceful outcome to the war even harder to achieve.

Analysts suggest the failure of these truces is ultimately tied to the political ambitions of the warring leaders – Lieutenant General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan of the SAF and the RSF’s head Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.

Fathi Abu Ammar, a Sudanese academic and editor-in-chief of Al-Wasat newspaper, argued that the military leadership is deliberately stalling negotiations to maintain its grip on power.

“All these efforts that serve the interest of the Sudanese people primarily were rejected by the army, rejected by al-Burhan and Yasser al-Atta (chief of staff of the SAF), and they all tried to obstruct them by setting broad lines for the peace they want,” Abu Ammar told Al Jazeera.

He said recent comments from the two military commanders hint that al-Burhan is preparing to formalise his rule over Sudan, perhaps for decades.

Supporters of SAF believe that after a series of victories on the battlefield, it is now operating from a position of strength and does not need to compromise.

Mohammed Ibrahim al-Rashid, director of the Center for International Political Relations Studies (Ma’alim), believes the RSF is facing a comprehensive defeat and that an SAF victory will end the war.

“The defeat now is not military; the defeat is diplomatic, a defeat in the corridors of the Security Council. The militia’s (RSF) load and its support are now in a critical position,” al-Rashid told Al Jazeera.

“Therefore, the government is reassured as days go by with the military advance … we can talk about breakthroughs with … a peace that achieves the interest of the Sudanese people, not one that reproduces the crisis and reproduces the militia.”

While the fighting in Sudan continues, experts believe that international diplomatic efforts to end the war are essentially dead.

Cameron Hudson, former adviser to the US envoy to Sudan, believes that applying punitive measures while excluding the warring parties from negotiations is counterproductive.

“I think that there is one approach the United States has not tried since the beginning of this war, which is providing incentives and motives for peace. The United States used only pressures: Pressures through sanctions, and also accusations of using chemical weapons, and even pressure by ignoring both parties and not travelling to Sudan, and not inviting Sudanese officials to participate in international conferences,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.

“The issue of accumulating pressures one after another has not succeeded and has not worked, and therefore the United States must acknowledge that this approach has not succeeded. And until their position is revealed with the end of the war, I do not think that either of the fighting parties will proceed to stop the fighting.”

articles.title: Former Liverpool star Mohamed Salah given six-month driving ban
articles.summary: The former Liverpool footballer's Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding in Wilmslow in March.
articles.body:
Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.

Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents.

The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge.

He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court.

A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce.

The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team.

Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history".

He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season.

articles.title: Tehran threatens to use ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
articles.summary: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.
articles.body: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency. Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit. Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday. The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation. Trump also said he was still deciding how to proceed with the war, describing his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.” “My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up,” he said. “They better behave,” Trump warned. The president has previously said he did not believe the Iran war would end until after November’s midterm elections. He has also said oil prices would not come down until then. Oil prices slid to their lowest point in more than a week Monday as hopes for renewed talks between the U.S. and Iran grew, while signs of a recovery in Saudi crude exports eased supply concerns, despite continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. Trump told Fox News that Washington was in constant communication with the Houthis — and that the Yemeni rebel group had agreed not to fight with the U.S., Yingst reported. Trump has said that the administration had been in touch with the Houthis, but did not say when. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.” Violence escalated over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had used missiles and drones to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh on Saturday, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub. Meanwhile, fighting flared in southwest Yemen as the rebel group made gains against Saudi-backed forces. The New York Times reported Monday that the president had considered, but ultimately decided against on Sunday joining Saudi Arabia in joint strikes against the Houthis in Yemen. NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the newspaper’s reporting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “This is a really fluid situation,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America think tank who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, said Monday. He cautioned that he would not “rule out anything” when it comes to Trump’s stance on whether to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis. Shipping data showed 17 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, though Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers with their transponders off, Reuters reported. A total of 22 tankers, mainly very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, exited Hormuz in the week of Sept. 13, with Saudi Arabia and Iraq each accounting for 43% of the volume, the outlet reported, citing data from tracking group Kpler, which maintains the MarineTraffic website. Meanwhile, at least 51 vessels made the crossing along the Bab el Mandeb, with 33 vessels exiting the waterway over the weekend as the Houthis tightened their grip over the strait, the outlet reported. That was down from 57 vessels in the previous weekend. The Yemeni Health and Environment Ministry accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes targeting telecommunications towers in the Khabb wa ash-Sha’af district of Al-Jawf Governorate on Sunday that killed four telecommunications workers and injured three others. “Targeting essential service infrastructure, including telecommunications towers, constitutes a flagrant violation of international and humanitarian laws,” the ministry said in a post on Telegram. “It reveals the aggressor’s determination to disrupt basic services and exacerbate the suffering of the Yemeni people,” it said.

articles.title: Shocking discovery of ancient bones turns couple's kitchen renovation into 'crime scene'
articles.summary: A homeowner's kitchen renovation turned into a spooky police investigation after a builder unearthed Anglo-Saxon human bones roughly 1,000 years old.
articles.body: Ancient human remains that turned a couple's home renovation into a crime investigation have finally been laid to rest — with the homeowner recently speaking out about the ordeal. Ross Sledger, 49, was at work in spring 2019 when a builder working on a kitchen addition at his home unearthed what appeared to be human bones, news agency SWNS reported. The remains were formally re-interred this August during a ceremony at a church near Sledger's home in Wye, Kent, in southeastern England. ANCIENT 'SEATED' SKELETONS UNEARTHED BENEATH MODERN SCHOOL SITE, PUZZLING ARCHAEOLOGISTS Sledger said he initially thought little of the discovery, assuming the bones belonged to a farm animal or pet, SWNS reported. "[The builder] said, 'I’ve found some bones,' and I said, 'Great,' thinking it was farming or pets," Sledger said. Sledger said he was stunned to learn the remains could be human. "As you can imagine, a lot of language came out of my mouth. I was thinking, 'You must be joking, this is a wind-up,' but he said, 'I’m deadly serious,'" Sledger recalled. AIRBNB GUESTS CHECK INTO THEIR RENTAL TO FIND STARTLING DISCOVERY ON WALL The bones, later determined to be Anglo-Saxon remains roughly 1,000 years old, caused a stir — and a police investigation. Around 10 officers went to the home to sift through the backyard, with investigators eventually finding remains of a second body. "I was thinking, 'Oh no, this is going to delay it. I’ve got bricklayers next week.'" In all, the grisly discovery included a femur, two skulls, ribs, part of a pelvis and fragments of a humerus and finger bones. "They thought it was a crime scene," Sledger said. "They had to have an officer overnight, and every half hour he had to get out of his car." SISTERS IN VIRAL VIDEO REVEAL TRUTH IN ‘EERIE’ FAMILY PHOTO THEY DISCOVERED AT RENTAL HOME "That set off the neighbor's floodlights, which set off my dog barking. So as you can imagine, I didn’t get much sleep that night," he added, as SWNS noted. About 48 hours after the initial discovery, specialists confirmed the remains were ancient and not related to a modern-day crime. But the discoveries didn't end there. Sledger later uncovered what he described as "knuckles and fingers" while installing artificial grass in his backyard — which caused some renovation-related anxiety. "I was thinking, 'Oh no, this is going to delay it. I’ve got bricklayers next week,'" Sledger said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "I was thinking, 'This could take months,' but luckily, they were done and dusted by the end of the weekend, which was good." After the police investigation ended, Sledger said the remains were transferred to a historical society and eventually to a local vicar, though arranging their final resting place took time. "I think it was a question of getting permission and whether they would be allowed to be there," Sledger added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "I think it was a bit more red tape than anything else." At the August re-interment ceremony, the vicar chose the hymn "Jerusalem," which Sledger said offered a fitting tribute to the ancient remains. Sledger's backyard isn't the only one in the United Kingdom to yield an unexpected piece of history. The Hampshire couple uncovered a hoard of 70 historic English coins while adjusting a fence near a flower bed in 2020. articles.title: Council leader Jason Zadrozny found guilty of fraud and tax evasion
articles.summary: Jason Zadrozny, leader of Ashfield District Council in Nottinghamshire, is convicted of 13 offences.
articles.body:
Ashfield District Council leader Jason Zadrozny has been found guilty of fraud and tax evasion.

Zadrozny, of Stanton Hill, was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds.

Prosecutors also alleged he failed to pay tax on four rental properties.

The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion.

The verdicts came after a jury at Northampton Crown Court had deliberated for nearly 11 hours.

Zadrozny was told by the judge he will be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence".

Thanking jury members for their "care and attention" during the trial, the judge added the council leader would be given unconditional bail until his sentencing hearing.

During the trial, jurors were told Zadrozny had set up the Ashfield Heritage Society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council, which he then transferred into his personal account .

This included £7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny - who was a county councillor at the time - claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield".

The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March.

Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends.

They said the fraud came to light in March 2021, when Catherine Mason, who was hoping to stand for election in Ashfield, was looking into the council's expenditure and investigated the setting up of the heritage society.

The county council launched an investigation and subsequently passed the details on to the police.

articles.title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
articles.summary: Visitors stopping to take pictures of the 68m medieval embroidery were holding up others, prompting the rule change.
articles.body:
The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.

Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.

The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.

But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.

A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible.

"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."

The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.

British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux.

The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.

Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.

The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London.

Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.

Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.

Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum.

articles.title: Indiana man wants new trial in killing of teens with pagan ritual evidence introduced
articles.summary: A man serving 130 years in prison for killing two teen girls in Indiana is asking an appeals court to overturn his convictions, saying that he confessed while he was having a psychological crisis and was unfairly barred from arguing at trial that the girls were killed by unknown participants in a pagan ritual.
articles.body: A man serving 130 years in prison for killing two teen girls in Indiana is asking an appeals court to overturn his convictions, saying that he confessed while he was having a psychological crisis and was unfairly barred from arguing at trial that the girls were killed by unknown participants in a pagan ritual. Jurors convicted Richard Allen of murder in 2024 in the deaths of Abigail Williams, 13, and Liberty German, 14, known as Abby and Libby. The case in the tiny town of Delphi went unsolved for more than five years before Allen was arrested, becoming a magnet for true-crime enthusiasts. Allen’s case goes before the Indiana Court of Appeals for an hour of arguments on Monday. Prosecutors said some of Allen’s incriminating statements came before he showed signs of mental illness and continued after he improved. Even without his confessions, they said jurors had enough evidence to find Allen guilty. They said Allen admitted to being on the trail near where the girls were killed at the time one of them took a brief video of a suspicious man nearby saying, “Down the hill.” Prosecutors said that if the judge had allowed a defense expert to testify about a possible pagan ritual it would have turned the trial into a sideshow. Unusual evidence found along with bodies of the teens The girls’ bodies were found down a steep hill from an abandoned railroad trestle on a hiking trail just outside of Delphi on Feb. 13, 2017. The eighth graders were dropped off and never made it to their pickup point. The teens’ throats were cut, and a few branches were scattered over their bodies. One was found nude while the other was wearing the first victim’s clothes. There was no evidence they had been sexually assaulted. Prosecutors said Allen was armed with a gun and forced the girls off the hiking trail. They said he confessed to planning to rape them before a passing van made him change his mind and he killed them. An expert testified an unspent bullet found between the teens’ bodies “had been cycled through” Allen’s handgun. Defense lawyers at his trial said no witness explicitly identified Allen as the man seen near the trail the afternoon the girls went missing. They also said no fingerprint, DNA or forensic evidence linked Allen to the murder scene. Allen’s lawyers say isolation led to mental breakdown and false confessions Allen was held in solitary confinement while awaiting trial. He denied killing the girls for months, but his attorneys said mental stress from isolation led to a steep psychological decline. Eventually, his mental state became so bad he convinced himself he killed the girls and confessed several times, his lawyers said. “Allen lost forty pounds, was unable to care for himself, was tased, his face was black and blue and at times bleeding, and he was poisoned by fecal matter and toilet water,” attorneys Stacy Uliana and Mark Leeman wrote in their brief. Prosecutors said the statements coincided with Allen seeing evidence in the case including the conditions of the teens’ bodies. “The discovery materials forced Allen to face the horrifying evidence of what he did ... images and events he had been able to ignore and repress over the five years in which his guilt had gone undiscovered,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita wrote in his office’s brief. Expert on pagan killings not allowed to testify Allen’s trial attorneys wanted to put an expert witness on the stand to testify the killings appeared to be a ritual sacrifice by people who worshipped Odin, the king of the gods in Norse mythology. The expert was expected to say the positioning of the bodies, the branches on the remains, the outdoor location of the crime and knife wounds to the victims all were indications of pagan rituals. Prosecutors said the expert had limited examples and that defense lawyers shouldn’t be able to present just any theory without evidence to back it up. Other issues Allen’s attorneys are expected to argue before the appeals court are inconsistencies in how witnesses described the suspicious man near the trail, pointing to a sketch of a potential suspect that didn’t look like Allen. They also question why an expert for Allen’s defense wasn’t allowed to question whether marks on an unfired bullet can be traced to a specific gun.

articles.title: German Chancellor Merz fights to survive historic defeat in regional elections
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced a struggle to stabilize his position and keep his agenda on track Monday after voters inflicted two more defeats on his party, ejecting it from a state legislature for the first time in its eight-decade history.
articles.body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced a struggle to stabilize his position and keep his agenda on track Monday after voters inflicted two more defeats on his party, ejecting it from a state legislature for the first time in its eight-decade history. The unpopular Merz vowed to stay on and push through reforms to Germany, Europe’s biggest economy, minutes after polls closed Sunday in regional elections in Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural eastern region on the Baltic Sea coast. Still, final results underlined the extent of what Merz conceded was a “disaster” in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. His center-right Christian Democratic Union fell just below the 5% of the vote needed to keep seats in the regional parliament, the first time that has happened in 77 years of modern Germany’s federal republic, after losing more than half its support. The CDU also dropped to second place in Berlin behind the hard-left Left Party, which is in pole position to lead the next city government — though Merz’s party could, depending on how coalition talks go, still retain city hall. A far-right party gains again Neither state is one of Germany’s political heavyweights. The CDU’s 2023 win in Berlin was its only one in the past 25 years in the capital, which has tended to lean left, and the party was already weak in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. But the manner of its defeat in the latter in particular adds to the headwinds Merz faces after a stinging defeat by the far-right Alternative for Germany two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt, another region in the formerly communist east, damaged his authority and set off speculation that he might be replaced. Alternative for Germany, or AfD, emerged as the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but the center-left Social Democrats — the junior party in Merz’s national governing coalition — were fairly close behind after a campaign focused squarely on the state governor, Manuela Schwesig, as a bulwark against the far-right party. That polarization helped squeeze other mainstream parties, including the CDU. A left-leaning three-party coalition under Schwesig would have a majority in the new regional legislature. Questions over how Germany should be reformed Schwesig and others in the governing parties have cast doubt on aspects of the federal government’s reform agenda, which is meant to bolster a chronically sluggish economy. The reform plans include a potentially painful overhaul of the creaking pension system, a reduction of Germany’s stifling bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for low- and middle-income families. The Social Democrats’ national leaders said Monday that they stand by the coalition. But they made clear that they will seek at least some changes to the plans. Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, who is also the finance minister, said that “saying we will ignore what voters told us in three state elections won’t work.” “We need reforms, but these reforms must be fair and they need support in the population,” he said. The party’s other co-leader, Labor Minister Bärbel Bas, said the plans need a “reality check” and a “fairness check,” but that she was optimistic of finding solutions on the pension system reform, the most controversial plan. “There would be nothing more lethal than letting this coalition break apart over some technical question,” Bas said. Merz faces more meetings Monday with his party’s leadership. Much will depend on the CDU’s influential regional leaders; the party’s eight state governors last week backed the chancellor, though questions remained about how wholehearted their support was. There are at least no more electoral tests this year. However, five state elections are scheduled next year, three of them in April. They include one in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, currently led by a prominent CDU figure often cited as a possible successor to Merz, Hendrik Wüst. None of the five elections is in the east, where AfD is strongest. “I don’t see that swapping out a leadership figure would really bring a change,” Education Minister Karin Prien, who is also a deputy CDU leader, told Phoenix television, adding that she doesn’t see “another personnel offer” coming. “So we must now discuss with one another — together with the chancellor as a government, and on the other hand as a party — how we win more acceptance and more credibility among the population,” Prien said.
